To fix (1)

To fix Reproducibility Check

What we found

  • We assessed 4 R code files for reproducibility and ran them (each in an isolated Docker container).
  • 4 files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
  • 1 of 4 scripts ran without error when executed.
  • Of the others, 3 did not reproduce.
  • 11 installable dependencies detected.
  • We assessed 1 Python code file for reproducibility and ran it.
  • 0 of 1 Python script ran without error when executed.
  • Of the others, 1 did not reproduce.
  • 5 installable Python dependencies detected.
  • 25 statistics stored from the extracted output; 0 of 2 reported tests matched (0%).

Note

See the section Reproducibility Check below for the details.

To check (4)

To check Codebook Check

What we found

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 1310 extracted data columns.

Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 22 codebook/README/label sources and 1310 data columns across 91 files.

No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

To check Repository Check

What we found

  • We listed only part of 1 OSF project (the request limit was reached).
  • The OSF project https://osf.io/saqf2 is private. Metacheck examined the files through the view_only link. As the preprint is public, and the OSF Files are accessible to anyone, consider making the OSF project public.
  • We found 201 files in 3 repositories. The paper cites OSF.IO/3J9UT, osf.io/3527A only in its reference list; we checked them as the authors’ deposit for this paper. Linking them in the data availability statement as well makes them easier to find.
  • We found 22 README files and 1 repository without READMEs.
  • We could not classify 24 files.
  • We found 28 file naming problems to fix.
Show details

Partly Listed Repositories

1 OSF project (osf.io/3527A) has more folders than metacheck lists by default, so only part of its files were listed (83 files), and what this report says about its files describes only that part. Run the check again with cache = TRUE to list the next part, or raise osf_max_requests.

Private repositories checked through a view-only or peer-review link

The OSF project https://osf.io/saqf2 is private. Metacheck examined the files through the view_only link. As the preprint is public, and the OSF Files are accessible to anyone, consider making the OSF project public.

The paper cites OSF.IO/3J9UT, osf.io/3527A only in its reference list; we checked them as the authors’ deposit for this paper. Linking them in the data availability statement as well makes them easier to find.

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Consider depositing a requirements.txt that lists each package with its version (for example the output of pip freeze).

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

To check Data Check

What we found

  • We could not list every file of 1 repository, so the checks did not see all its files: osf.io/3527A (listed in part: the request limit was reached).
  • We classified 201 files: 77 data, 9 code, 28 documentation, 63 materials, 24 unknown.
  • We found 77 tabular data files and extracted 1310 columns from 67 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 3 study groups (ex1, ex2, ex3), plus 22 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).
  • 3 tabular data files could not be read because they were not downloaded. This can happen for private repositories or failed downloads; you can also pass local_path to point at a local copy.
  • 7 files read as a table but are not a usable rectangular dataset (Data Conversion Legend.xlsx: 80% of columns are free text, not variables; release 1.0/version 1.0/auxiliary files/reading task materials/supp texts.xlsx: 100% of columns are free text, not variables; release 1.0/version 1.0/auxiliary files/reading task materials/supp texts.csv: 100% of columns are free text, not variables; release 1.0/version 1.1/auxillary files/reading task materials/supp texts.xlsx: 100% of columns are free text, not variables; release 1.0/version 1.1/auxillary files/reading task materials/supp texts.csv: 100% of columns are free text, not variables; release 1.0/version 1.2/auxiliary files/reading task materials/supp texts.csv: 100% of columns are free text, not variables; release 1.0/version 1.2/auxiliary files/reading task materials/supp texts.xlsx: 100% of columns are free text, not variables). No columns were extracted and they were not sent to the LLM. Share the underlying data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable) with a codebook: Data Conversion Legend.xlsx, release 1.0/version 1.0/auxiliary files/reading task materials/supp texts.xlsx, release 1.0/version 1.0/auxiliary files/reading task materials/supp texts.csv, release 1.0/version 1.1/auxillary files/reading task materials/supp texts.xlsx, release 1.0/version 1.1/auxillary files/reading task materials/supp texts.csv, release 1.0/version 1.2/auxiliary files/reading task materials/supp texts.csv, release 1.0/version 1.2/auxiliary files/reading task materials/supp texts.xlsx. We ran automated data-quality checks on 1310 columns; 214 columns have at least one potential issue (129 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 34 columns with numeric values stored as text; 21 columns with inconsistent category casing; 11 columns of free text that may contain personal detail; 9 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long; 7 columns with leading/trailing whitespace; 6 columns with values in a legacy (non-UTF-8) encoding). We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender. 8 of 13 spreadsheet files have at least one formatting issue (colour coding, merged cells, empty rows/columns, or an offset header).
Show details

This module classifies repository files and, for tabular data files available locally, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

lang text_num back_trans
mo 1 In ancient Roman religion and mythology, Janus was the god of beginnings and entrances. He is typicallydepicted as having two faces, symbolizing his ability to look into both the past and the future. Janus can controlthe beginning and the end of conflicts, and therefore war and peace. The gates of his temple are opened duringtimes of war and closed during times of peace. As the god of doors, Janus is also associated with entering andexiting the home. Janus usually symbolizes change and transformation, such as moving from one state toanother, from one perspective to another, from immaturity to maturity. Therefore, Janus was worshipped at thetime of harvest and sowing, as well as marriage, death and at the beginning of other events. Janus does not havea specially appointed priest, but the high priest conducts his own rites. Janus represent the middle groundbetween the barbarism and civilization, the rural and the urban, the youth and the adulthood. Ancient Greekshad no gods comparable to Janus, so the Romans declared him as a special god in their culture.
mo 2 Shaka sign is related to Hawaii and surfing culture, and it is a gesture of friendship. The gesture is to bend the thumb and little finger, while closing the middle three fingers, with the back of the hand facing outward to show respect. In the 1960s, visiting surfers referred to the local culture and customs of Hawaii and used the Shaka signal. It is widely used worldwide. It is mainly used as a signal of bow or gratitude, and to express praise from one person to another. Hawaiian residents use the Shaka sign to represent the “Aloha Spirit”, representing the concepts of friendship, understanding, compassion, and unity between different ethnic cultures. Although the exact origin of this symbol is not yet clear, some people believe that its origin comes from Spanish immigrants. To show a friendly attitude, they folded their middle finger and placed their thumb on their lips. This also means they share drinks with the indigenous people they encounter in Hawaii.
mo 3 In competitive sports, doping refers to the use of prohibited drugs by athletes to enhance their athletic performance. The term “doping” is widely used by organizations that regulate sporting competition. The use of doping is widely considered unethical and is frowned upon by a number of major organizations, including the International Olympic Committee. The open cheating and wrongdoing of athletes, who avoid detection by taking obvious measures, has made the moral rebellion even more serious. Although athletes using doping are often in the headlines these days, it is not a new phenomenon. In fact, it is as old as sport itself. For many years, athletes have held different opinions on doping, from the use of drugs in ancient chariot races to recent controversies in baseball and cycling. In recent decades, authorities and sports organizations have tried to strictly regulate drug use in sports. The main reasons behind the ban are the health risks of performance-enhancing drugs, equal opportunities for athletes, and setting a positive example of drug-free sports for the public. Anti-doping authorities repeatedly emphasize that the use of performance-enhancing drugs goes against the “spirit of sport”.
mo 4 The thylacine was the largest carnivorous marsupial in modern times. It is known as Tasmanian tigers because of its tiger-like stripes. Also known as the Tasmanian wolf due to its appearance and characteristics. This kind of animal is widely distributed in the subtropical rainforest of New Guinea, the Australian grassland, Tasmania and other places. Later, humans regarded it as an enemy and carried out large-scale massacres under the government reward system. Like other marsupials, thylacine have a pouch in their female body, and undeveloped cubs develop in the pouch after birth. The male thylacine also has a small bag that can protect its external genitalia when it runs out of the bushes. It is said that the thylacine wolf has a large mouth opening, swollen muscles and bones in its stomach, and eats a lot. In modern times, people have been searching for the trail of the thylacine, but there is no conclusive evidence to prove its existence. Therefore, the scientific community generally believes that the wolf bag has become extinct.
mo 5 The United Nations designates June 5th as World Environment Day every year. As the main force for global residents to raise environmental awareness and encourage environmental action, and through this important social movement, to raise people’s awareness of emerging environmental issues such as marine pollution and global warming. Currently, more than 100 countries around the world participate in World Environment Day every year, with the aim of raising public awareness of the concept. Every year on World Environment Day, major companies, non-governmental organizations, various groups, governments, and social celebrities around the world actively advocate for environmental issues based on the new themes selected during the year. For example, with the theme of ” Beat Plastic Pollution” calls for the implementation of plastic reduction actions in everyone’s daily life, abandoning the habit of simplification, and minimizing the use of plastic products.
mo 6 Monocle glasses are corrective lenses used only to correct or enhance the vision of one eye. It consists of a circular lens, usually with a metal ring on the circumference, connected to a rope or wire. Then connect the other end of the rope to the clothes wearing glasses to avoid loss. In the late 19th century, monocular glasses were usually owned by wealthy upper class men. Combined with a Frock coat and a top hat, the monocle glasses formed the capitalist clothing in the stereotype of the late nineteenth century. Single lens glasses were also the attire of military officers during this period. Although monocular glasses were popular in the late 19th century, they are now very rare. This is largely thanks to the advancement of optics. Refraction can better measure anisometropia. So each one is equipped with glasses and contact lenses of different strength.
mo 7 Wine tasting is the act of testing and evaluating grape alcohol. Although the practice of grape alcohol tasting is as noble as the making of alcohol, the theory of the method was gradually established before the end of the Middle Ages. Today, professional wine tasters use special names to describe the taste, aroma, and general characteristics of grape wine. In recent years, there have been challenges to the credibility of wine experts and consumer tastings. For example, studies have shown that people expect expensive wines to have more attractive characteristics than relatively inexpensive wines: when sommeliers are mistakenly told that a wine is more expensive, they almost always say that it tastes better than a wine of the same price but identified as less expensive. Other studies have also shown that the judgments of wine tasters may be biased by their knowledge of wine details such as origin, reputation, or other considerations. Therefore, tasting wine objectively requires blind tasting, which means that tasters cannot first look at the label or bottle shape. Blind tasting may also involve serving wine in black glasses to conceal its color.
mo 8 Orange juice is juice extracted from orange flesh. Merchants, in order to extend the shelf life of orange juice, remove oxygen from the juice while killing Pasteurella. But this greatly reduces the taste of the juice, so some spices are usually added. In addition, some fruit juices are dried and hydrated, or concentrated and further processed with water. Although orange juice contains a large amount of vitamins, it also contains high concentrations of monosaccharides, no less than soft drinks. Therefore, the health value of orange juice is highly controversial, and some governments have adjusted their nutritional recommendations to encourage the use of slow-digested fruits instead of orange juice, and limit daily consumption.
mo 9 Beekeeping refers to the artificial breeding of bees. The most commonly cultivated species are bees that can produce honey. Can be sold to other beekeepers. Ancient Egypt has a history of beekeeping. From Egyptian art more than 4,000 years ago, it can be seen that people used simple hives and smoke to keep bees, and stored honey in jars, and some sealed honeypots also It was regarded as a funerary object of the pharaoh and placed in the tomb. The method of raising bees with artificial hives has been handed down since ancient times, and it has been used until the eighteenth century. It was not until the biology of bees was better understood that this prompted Europeans to invent movable hives. Since then, harvesting honey does not need to destroy the entire hive. Recent studies have found that beekeepers have higher levels of antibodies to bee venom than normal people, which is consistent with the belief of some beekeepers that being stung by bees a few times a season can ensure the safety of beekeepers.
mo 10 A national flag is a symbol of a country. The national flag displayed represents the sovereignty of a country. The historical origin of the national flag is the military flag used for identification during ancient wars. Since the early 17th century, the national flag has been widely used outside the battlefield. Nowadays, the national flag is often hung inside and outside government buildings, and citizens also use it in different occasions. The shape and size ratio of the national flag are usually prescribed by a country’s constitution. The Aspect ratio of national flags varies from country to country, but most of them are rectangular, and the width does not exceed its height. In the world, only Switzerland and the Vatican have square flags, while Nepal is the only country with a triangular flag. The color and logo of the national flag have special meanings in design and should represent the special logo of the country, but many national flags have similar colors and designs. Red, white, green, and blue are commonly used in the national flag.
mo 11 The International Union for Conservation of Nature is an international organization dedicated to nature conservation and sustainable use of natural resources. This institution is involved in data collection, analysis, research, field investigations, publicity work, and educational work. Its doctrine is “to protect nature through global social influence, encouragement, and support, so that the utilization of natural resources is both fair and ecologically sustainable”. In the past few decades, the organization has expanded its focus from ecological protection to other areas, and now includes issues related to sustainable development in its budget. The difference between this organization and other international environmental organizations is that it does not aim to mobilize support for nature conservation, but rather to influence the actions of governments, businesses, and other stakeholders by providing information and advice, as well as establishing partnerships. The organization is widely recognized by the public for compiling and publishing the “Red List of Endangered Species” to assess the Conservation status of global species. Today, the organization employs approximately 1000 full-time employees in over 50 countries.
mo 12 A license plate are metal or plastic signs hung for official confirmation purposes. All countries require the registration of road machines such as minibuses, trucks, and motorcycles for transportation license plates. The need for other means of transportation such as bicycles, boats, or tractors varies depending on the management authority. The license plate used for registration is a series of letters and numbers, which can be used to identify the owner registered in the license plate issuance area. In some countries, each license plate number is unique throughout the country, while in others, the license plate number is unique within a state or province. France was the first country to adopt license plate at the end of the 19th century. In the early 20th century, license plate varied in size and shape depending on the jurisdiction in which they were located. Therefore, if car owners left the jurisdiction, they needed to drill new holes in the vehicle to hang the new license plate. In the late 1950s, standardized license plates emerged after agreements were reached between vehicle manufacturers, governments, and international organizations.

mo 1 Janus ᠡᠷᠲᠡᠨ ᠤ ᠷᠤᠮᠠ ᠢᠢᠨ ᠱᠠᠰᠢᠨ ᠰᠤᠷᠳᠠᠬᠤᠨ ᠪᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠰᠢᠳᠢᠲᠤ ᠦᠯᠢᠭᠡᠷ ᠲᠤ᠂ ᠵᠡᠢᠨᠡᠰ ᠪᠤᠯ ᠲᠦᠮᠡᠨ ᠡᠬᠢᠯᠡᠯᠲᠡ ᠪᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠶᠡᠬᠡ ᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠨ ᠤ ᠪᠤᠷᠬᠠᠨ ᠪᠤᠯᠤᠨ᠎ᠠ᠃ ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠦᠩᠭᠡᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠡᠳᠦᠢ ᠢᠢ ᠨᠡᠪᠲᠡ ᠦᠵᠡᠳᠡᠭ ᠪᠤᠯᠬᠤᠷ᠂ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠳᠤ ᠬᠤᠶᠠᠳᠠᠮᠠᠯ ᠴᠢᠨᠠᠷ ᠲᠠᠢ ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠳ ᠬᠤᠶᠠᠷ ᠨᠢᠭᠤᠷ ᠲᠠᠢ ᠭᠡᠵᠤ ᠬᠦᠮᠦᠰ ᠦᠷᠭᠦᠯᠵᠢ ᠳᠦᠷᠰᠦᠯᠡᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠵᠡᠢᠨᠡᠰ ᠵᠦᠷᠢᠴᠡᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠡᠬᠢᠯᠡᠯᠲᠡ ᠳᠡᠭᠦᠰᠬᠡᠯ ᠢ ᠤᠳᠤᠷᠢᠳᠴᠤ ᠴᠢᠳᠠᠳᠠᠭ ᠤᠴᠢᠷ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠳᠠᠢᠨ ᠪᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠡᠩᠬᠡ ᠳᠠᠢᠪᠤᠩ ᠢ ᠴᠤ ᠵᠠᠬᠢᠷᠴᠤ ᠴᠢᠳᠠᠳᠠᠭ᠃ ᠳᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠰᠦᠮ ᠡ ᠢᠢᠨ ᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡ ᠨᠢ ᠲᠠᠢᠨ ᠤ ᠦᠶ ᠡ ᠳᠤ ᠨᠡᠭᠡᠭᠳᠡᠨ ᠲᠠᠢᠪᠤᠩ ᠴᠠᠭ ᠲᠤ ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠭᠳᠠᠳᠠᠭ᠃ ᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠨ ᠰᠠᠬᠢᠭᠤᠰᠤ ᠪᠤᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠬᠤᠪᠢ ᠳᠤ᠂ ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠪᠠᠰᠠ ᠭᠡᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠨ ᠤ ᠤᠷᠤᠵᠤ ᠭᠠᠷᠬᠤ ᠯᠤᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠬᠤᠯᠪᠤᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠲᠠᠢ᠃ ᠵᠠᠢᠨᠠᠰ ᠶᠡᠷᠦᠳᠡ ᠪᠡᠨ ᠬᠤᠪᠢᠷᠠᠯᠲᠠ ᠪᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠰᠢᠯᠵᠢᠯᠲᠡ ᠢᠢ ᠪᠡᠯᠭᠡᠳᠡᠳᠡᠭ᠂ ᠵᠢᠱᠢᠶᠡᠯᠡᠪᠡᠯ ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠪᠠᠢᠳᠠᠯ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠨᠦᠭᠦᠭᠡ ᠪᠠᠢᠳᠠᠯ  ᠳᠤ ᠤᠷᠤᠬᠤ ᠬᠤᠪᠢᠷᠠᠯᠲᠠ᠂ ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠭᠠᠰᠤ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠨᠦᠭᠦᠭᠡ ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠭᠠᠰᠤᠨ ᠳᠤ ᠤᠴᠢᠬᠤ ᠰᠢᠯᠵᠢᠯᠲᠡ᠂ ᠪᠠᠯᠴᠢᠷ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠢᠳᠡᠷ ᠪᠤᠯᠬᠤ ᠦᠰᠦᠯᠲᠡ  ᠵᠡᠷᠭᠡ ᠢᠢ ᠪᠡᠯᠭᠡᠳᠡᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠶᠠᠭ ᠢᠢᠮᠦ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠵᠠᠢᠨᠡᠰ ᠢ ᠡᠯᠪᠡᠭ ᠬᠤᠷᠢᠶᠠᠯᠲᠠ ᠢᠢᠨ ᠦᠶ ᠡ ᠪᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠳᠠᠷᠢᠯᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠢᠢᠨ ᠬᠤᠭᠤᠴᠠᠭᠠ ᠤ ᠡᠬᠢᠨ ᠤ ᠦᠶ ᠡ ᠳᠤ ᠰᠦᠰᠦᠭ᠍ᠯᠡᠨ ᠳᠠᠬᠢᠵᠤ᠂ ᠤᠷᠤᠭ ᠬᠤᠷᠢᠮ᠂ ᠦᠬᠦᠯ ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠴᠠᠯ ᠵᠢᠴᠢ ᠪᠤᠰᠤᠳ ᠡᠬᠢᠯᠡᠯᠲᠡ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠴᠠᠭ ᠲᠤ ᠴᠤ ᠠᠳᠠᠯᠢᠬᠠᠨ ᠰᠦᠰᠦᠭᠯᠡᠵᠤ ᠪᠠᠢᠳᠠᠭ᠃ ᠵᠠᠢᠨᠡᠰ ᠲᠤ ᠳᠤᠰᠬᠠᠢ ᠳᠤᠬᠢᠷᠠᠭᠤᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠳᠠᠬᠢᠯᠠᠭᠴᠢ ᠪᠠᠢᠳᠠᠭ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ᠂ ᠬᠠᠷᠢᠨ ᠲᠡᠷᠢᠭᠦᠨ ᠳᠠᠬᠢᠯᠠᠭᠴᠢ ᠨᠢ ᠦᠪᠡᠷᠲᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠤ ᠶᠤᠰᠤᠯᠠᠯ ᠢ ᠭᠠᠷᠳᠠᠨ ᠬᠢᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠵᠠᠢᠨᠡᠰ ᠵᠡᠷᠯᠢᠭ ᠪᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠪᠤᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤᠨ ᠂ ᠬᠦᠳᠡᠭᠡ ᠪᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠬᠤᠳᠠ᠂ ᠵᠠᠯᠠᠭᠤᠴᠤᠳ ᠪᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠲᠤᠮᠤᠴᠤᠤᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠬᠣᠭᠣᠷᠣᠨᠳᠤᠬᠢ ᠵᠠᠪᠰᠠᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠪᠠᠢᠳᠠᠯ ᠢ ᠳᠦᠯᠦᠭᠡᠯᠡᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠡᠷᠲᠡᠨ ᠤ ᠭᠷᠢᠭ ᠲᠤ ᠵᠠᠢᠨᠤᠰ ᠲᠠᠢ ᠮᠦᠷᠦ ᠵᠡᠷᠭᠡᠴᠡᠬᠦ ᠰᠠᠬᠢᠭᠤᠯᠰᠤᠨ ᠪᠠᠢᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ ᠪᠣᠯᠬᠣᠷ ᠷᠤᠮᠠᠴᠤᠳ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠥᠪᠡᠷ ᠦᠨ ᠬᠢᠨ ᠰᠣᠶᠣᠯ ᠳᠤ ᠲᠤᠰᠬᠠᠢ ᠣᠷᠣᠰᠢᠳᠠᠭ ᠪᠤᠷᠬᠠᠨ ᠬᠡᠮᠡᠨ ᠵᠠᠷᠯᠠᠨ ᠲᠤᠩᠬᠠᠯᠠᠳᠠᠭ᠃
mo 2 Shaka ᠱᠠᠺᠠ ᠳᠤᠬᠢᠶ ᠠ ᠨᠢ ᠬᠠᠸᠠᠶ᠋ᠢ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠨ ᠳᠠᠪᠠᠯᠭᠠᠨ ᠭᠤᠯᠭᠤᠯᠲᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠰᠣᠶᠣᠯ ᠲᠠᠶ ᠬᠣᠯᠪᠣᠭᠳᠠᠳᠠᠭ ᠨᠥᠬᠥᠷᠰᠡᠭ ᠰᠡᠳᠬᠢᠯ ᠢ ᠢᠯᠡᠳᠬᠡᠬᠦ ᠭᠠᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠳᠤᠬᠢᠶ ᠡ ᠪᠤᠯᠤᠨ᠎ᠠ᠃ ᠲᠤᠰ ᠳᠤᠬᠢᠶ ᠡ ᠨᠢ ᠡᠷᠡᠬᠡᠢ ᠬᠤᠷᠤᠭᠤ ᠪᠠ ᠰᠢᠭᠡᠵᠡᠢ ᠬᠤᠷᠤᠭᠤ ᠪᠠᠨ ᠭᠤᠵᠢᠢᠯᠭᠠᠬᠤ ᠢᠢᠨ ᠬᠠᠮᠲᠤ ᠳᠤᠮᠳᠠᠬᠢ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠬᠤᠷᠤᠭᠤ ᠪᠡᠨ ᠬᠤᠮᠢᠵᠤ᠂ ᠭᠠᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠠᠷᠤ ᠦᠪᠦᠷ ᠲᠠᠯ᠎ᠠ ᠪᠠᠨ ᠬᠠᠨᠳᠤᠭᠤᠯᠤᠨ ᠶᠤᠰᠤᠯᠠᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠳᠤᠬᠢᠶ ᠡ ᠦᠭᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠬᠤᠷᠢᠳ᠋ᠤᠭᠠᠷ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠵᠢᠷᠠᠭᠠᠳ ᠣᠨ ᠳᠤ᠂ ᠠᠢᠯᠠᠴᠢᠯᠠᠨ ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠳᠠᠪᠠᠯᠭᠠᠨ ᠭᠤᠯᠭᠤᠭᠴᠢᠳ ᠬᠠᠸᠠᠶ᠋ᠢ  ᠶᠢᠨ ᠤᠷᠤᠨ ᠨᠤᠲᠤᠭ ᠤᠨ ᠰᠣᠶᠣᠯ ᠪᠠ ᠵᠠᠩ ᠳᠠᠳᠬᠠᠯ  ᠠᠴᠠ ᠡᠰᠢᠯᠡᠨ ᠱᠠᠺᠠ ᠳᠣᠬᠢᠶ᠎ᠠ ᠶᠢ ᠬᠡᠷᠡᠭ᠍ᠯᠡᠵᠡᠢ᠃ ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠨᠢ ᠳᠡᠯᠡᠬᠡᠶ  ᠶᠢᠨ ᠬᠡᠪᠴᠢᠶᠡᠨ ᠳᠤ ᠦᠷᠭᠡᠨ ᠬᠡᠷᠡᠭ᠍ᠯᠡᠭ᠍ᠳᠡᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠭᠣᠣᠯᠳᠠᠭᠤ ᠶᠤᠰᠤᠯᠠᠬᠤ ᠪᠤᠶᠤ ᠲᠠᠯᠠᠷᠬᠠᠬᠤ ᠳᠤᠬᠢᠶ ᠠ᠂ ᠲᠡᠷᠡᠴᠢᠯᠡᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠬᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠨᠦᠭᠦᠭᠡ ᠬᠦᠮᠦᠨ ᠳᠤ ᠬᠠᠨᠳᠤᠭᠤᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠮᠠᠭᠳᠠᠭᠠᠯ ᠢᠢᠡᠨ ᠢᠯᠡᠳᠬᠡᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠬᠠᠸᠠᠶ᠋ᠢ ᠵᠢᠨ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠭᠠᠯᠢ ᠠᠷᠠᠳ ᠱᠠᠺᠠ ᠳᠣᠬᠢᠶ᠎ᠠ ᠪᠠᠷ ᠠᠳᠠᠯᠢ ᠪᠤᠰᠤ ᠠᠷᠠᠰᠤᠲᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠰᠣᠶᠣᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠬᠣᠭᠣᠷᠣᠨᠳᠣᠬᠢ ᠨᠥᠬᠥᠷᠯᠡᠯ᠂ ᠣᠶᠢᠯᠠᠭᠠᠯᠲᠠ᠂ ᠬᠦᠭᠡᠷᠦᠭᠦᠢᠯᠡᠯ ᠪᠠ ᠪᠦᠯᠬᠦᠮᠳᠡᠯ ᠦᠨ ᠤᠬᠠᠭᠳᠠᠬᠤᠨ ᠢ ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠭᠤᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠠᠯᠤᠬ᠎ᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠵᠣᠷᠢᠭ ᠰᠠᠨᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠶᠢ ᠢᠯᠡᠳᠬᠡᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠬᠡᠳᠦᠶᠢᠪᠡᠷ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠬᠦ ᠪᠡᠯᠭᠡ ᠲᠡᠮᠳᠡᠭ ᠦᠨ ᠣᠨᠣᠪᠴᠢᠲᠠᠶ ᠡᠭᠦᠰᠦᠯ ᠨᠢ ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠬᠠᠨ ᠲᠣᠳᠣᠷᠬᠠᠶ ᠪᠢᠰᠢ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠴᠤ ᠵᠠᠷᠢᠮ ᠬᠥᠮᠦᠰ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠦ ᠡᠭᠦᠰᠦᠯ ᠨᠢ ᠢᠰᠫᠠᠨᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠨᠡᠭᠦᠳᠡᠯᠴᠢᠳ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠢᠷᠡᠯᠲᠡᠶ ᠭᠡᠵᠦ ᠦᠵᠡᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠨᠥᠬᠥᠷᠰᠡᠭ ᠣᠪᠣᠷ ᠢᠢᠡᠨ ᠢᠯᠡᠳᠬᠡᠬᠦ ᠢᠢᠨ ᠳᠤᠯᠠᠳᠠ ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠨᠠᠷ ᠳᠤᠮᠳᠠᠬᠢ ᠬᠤᠷᠤᠭᠤ ᠪᠠᠨ ᠨᠤᠭᠤᠯᠵᠤ᠂ ᠡᠷᠡᠬᠡᠶ ᠬᠤᠷᠤᠭᠤ ᠪᠠᠨ ᠤᠷᠤᠭᠤᠯ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ᠎ᠡ ᠪᠡᠨ ᠲᠠᠯᠪᠢᠳᠠᠭ᠃ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠨᠢ ᠮᠦᠨᠴᠤ ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠨ ᠦ ᠬᠠᠸᠠᠶ᠋ᠢ ᠳ᠋ᠤ ᠤᠴᠠᠷᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠤᠤᠭᠠᠯ ᠠᠷᠠᠳ ᠲᠡᠶ ᠤᠮᠳᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠢᠢᠡᠨ ᠬᠤᠪᠢᠶᠠᠯᠴᠠᠬᠤ ᠢᠢ ᠲᠥᠯᠥᠭᠡᠯᠡᠵᠦ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠳᠠᠭ ᠃

mo 4 Thylacine ᠤᠭᠤᠲᠠᠲᠤ ᠴᠢᠨᠣ᠎ᠠ ᠪᠣᠯ ᠣᠶᠢᠷ᠎ᠠ ᠦᠶ᠎ᠡ  ᠶᠢᠨ ᠬᠠᠮᠤᠭ ᠲᠣᠮᠣ ᠮᠢᠬᠠᠴᠢᠨ ᠤᠭᠤᠲᠠᠲᠤ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ ᠃ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠦ ᠪᠡᠶ᠎ᠡ ᠳᠡᠬᠢ ᠡᠷᠢᠶᠡᠨ ᠰᠤᠳᠠᠰᠤ ᠨᠢ ᠪᠠᠷᠰ ᠲᠠᠶ ᠲᠥᠰᠲᠡᠶ ᠲᠤᠯᠠ ᠪᠠᠰᠠ ᠲᠠᠰᠮᠠᠨᠢᠶ᠎ᠠ ᠪᠠᠷᠰ ᠭᠡᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠪᠠᠰᠠ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠦ ᠭᠠᠳᠠᠷ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠳᠠᠯ ᠪᠠ ᠣᠨᠴᠠᠯᠢᠭ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠲᠠᠰᠮᠠᠨᠢᠶ᠎ᠠ ᠴᠢᠨᠣ᠎ᠠ ᠭᠡᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠬᠦ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ ᠨᠢ ᠰᠢᠨ᠎ᠡ ᠬᠢᠨ᠋ᠸᠶᠠ  ᠶᠢᠨ ᠬᠠᠯᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠪᠦᠰᠡᠨ ᠦ ᠪᠣᠷᠣᠭᠠᠨᠲᠤ ᠣᠶ᠂ ᠠᠦ᠋ᠰᠲ᠋ᠷᠠᠯᠢᠶ᠎ᠠ  ᠶᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠯ᠎ᠠ ᠨᠤᠲᠤᠭ᠂ ᠲᠠᠰᠮᠠᠨᠢᠶ᠎ᠠ ᠠᠷᠠᠯ ᠵᠡᠷᠭᠡ ᠭᠠᠵᠠᠷ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠥᠷᠭᠡᠨ ᠲᠠᠷᠬᠠᠵᠤ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠵᠠᠶ᠃ ᠬᠣᠵᠢᠮ ᠨᠢ ᠬᠥᠮᠦᠨ ᠲᠥᠷᠥᠯᠬᠢᠲᠡᠨ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢ ᠳᠠᠶᠢᠰᠤᠨ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠦᠵᠡᠵᠦ᠂ ᠵᠠᠰᠠᠭ ᠤᠨ ᠣᠷᠳᠣᠨ ᠤ ᠱᠠᠩᠨᠠᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠳᠦᠷᠢᠮ ᠦᠨ ᠳᠣᠣᠷ᠎ᠠ ᠶᠡᠬᠡ ᠬᠡᠮᠵᠢᠶ᠎ᠡ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠬᠢᠲᠤᠨ ᠠᠯᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠪᠠᠢᠨ᠎ᠠ᠃ᠤᠭᠤᠲᠠᠲᠤ ᠴᠢᠨᠣ᠎ᠠ ᠨᠢ ᠪᠤᠰᠤᠳ ᠤᠭᠤᠲᠠᠲᠤ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ ᠲᠠᠶ ᠠᠳᠠᠯᠢ ᠪᠠᠷ ᠡᠮᠡᠭ᠍ᠴᠢᠨ ᠦ ᠪᠡᠶ᠎ᠡ ᠳᠦᠨᠢ ᠬᠡᠦᠬᠡᠳ ᠪᠣᠶᠢᠵᠢᠭᠤᠯᠬᠤ ᠤᠭᠤᠲᠠ ᠲᠠᠶ᠂ ᠪᠣᠶᠢᠵᠢᠭᠠᠳᠤᠶ ᠵᠤᠯᠵᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠠᠮᠢᠲᠠᠨ ᠢ ᠲᠥᠷᠥᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠦ ᠳᠠᠷᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠬᠡᠦᠬᠡᠳ ᠪᠣᠶᠢᠵᠢᠭᠤᠯᠬᠤ ᠤᠭᠤᠲᠠᠨ ᠳᠤ ᠪᠣᠶᠢᠵᠢᠭᠤᠯᠳᠠᠭ᠃ ᠡᠷ᠎ᠡ ᠤᠭᠤᠲᠠᠲᠤ ᠴᠢᠨᠣ᠎ᠠ ᠳᠤ ᠪᠠᠰᠠ ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠵᠢᠵᠢᠭ ᠤᠭᠤᠲᠠ ᠲᠠᠶ᠂ ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠨᠢ ᠪᠣᠳᠠ ᠮᠣᠳᠣᠨ ᠤ ᠳᠤᠮᠳᠠᠭᠤᠷ ᠭᠦᠶᠦᠵᠦ ᠭᠠᠷᠬᠤ ᠦᠶ᠎ᠡ ᠳᠦ ᠭᠠᠳᠠᠷ ᠪᠡᠯᠭᠡ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠡᠷᠬᠡᠲᠡᠨ  ᠢ ᠨᠢ ᠬᠠᠮᠠᠭᠠᠯᠠᠳᠠᠭ᠃ ᠬᠥᠮᠥᠰ ᠦᠨ ᠶᠠᠷᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠳᠤ ᠤᠭᠤᠲᠠᠲᠤ ᠴᠢᠨᠣ᠎ᠠ ᠠᠮᠠ ᠪᠠᠨ ᠠᠩᠭᠠᠶᠢᠬᠤ ᠬᠡᠮᠵᠢᠶ᠎ᠡ ᠨᠢ ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠶᠡᠬᠡ᠂ ᠭᠡᠳᠡᠰᠦᠨ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷᠡᠬᠢ ᠪᠤᠯᠴᠢᠩ ᠪᠠ ᠠᠷᠤᠭ ᠶᠠᠰᠤ ᠨᠢ ᠴᠢᠨᠦᠷᠡᠨ ᠲᠣᠮᠣᠷᠠᠵᠤ ᠶᠡᠬᠡ ᠬᠡᠮᠵᠢᠶᠡᠨ ᠦ ᠢᠳᠡᠰᠢ ᠢᠳᠡᠳᠡᠭ ᠭᠡᠨ᠎ᠡ᠃ ᠥᠢᠷ᠎ᠠ ᠦᠶ᠎ᠡ ᠳᠦ ᠬᠥᠮᠦᠰ ᠤᠭᠤᠲᠠᠲᠤ ᠴᠢᠨᠣ᠎ᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠥᠷ ᠢ ᠬᠠᠶᠢᠭᠰᠠᠭᠠᠷ ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠴᠤ ᠮᠥᠨ ᠯᠡ ᠣᠷᠣᠰᠢᠵᠤ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠬᠤ ᠶᠢ ᠭᠡᠷᠡᠴᠢᠯᠡᠬᠦ ᠪᠠᠲᠤᠲᠠᠶ ᠭᠡᠷᠡᠴᠢ ᠣᠯᠳᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠥᠬᠡᠶ᠂ ᠡᠶᠢᠮᠦ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠣᠳᠣᠬᠠᠨ ᠳᠤ ᠰᠢᠨᠵᠢᠯᠡᠬᠦ ᠤᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠬᠢᠨ ᠤᠭᠤᠲᠠᠲᠤ ᠴᠢᠨᠣ᠎ᠠ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨᠲᠡ ᠤᠰᠠᠳᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠭᠡᠵᠦ ᠨᠡᠶᠢᠳᠡᠮ ᠦᠵᠡᠵᠦ ᠪᠣᠶ᠃
mo 5 World Environment Day ᠤᠯᠠᠨ ᠤᠯᠤᠰ ᠤᠨ ᠬᠣᠯᠪᠣᠭᠠᠲᠤ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠭᠤᠯᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠠᠴᠠ ᠵᠢᠯ ᠪᠦᠷᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠵᠢᠷᠭᠤᠭᠠᠨ ᠰᠠᠷ᠎ᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠡᠳᠦᠷ ᠢ ᠳᠡᠯᠡᠬᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠣᠷᠴᠢᠨ ᠠᠬᠤᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠡᠳᠦᠷ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠲᠣᠭᠲᠠᠭᠠᠪᠠ᠃ ᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠳᠠᠮᠵᠢᠨ ᠪᠦᠬᠦ ᠪᠥᠮᠪᠥᠷᠴᠡᠭ ᠦᠨ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠭᠠᠯᠢ ᠠᠷᠠᠳ ᠤᠨ ᠣᠷᠴᠢᠨ ᠠᠬᠤᠶ ᠶᠢ ᠬᠠᠮᠠᠭᠠᠯᠠᠬᠤ ᠤᠬᠠᠮᠰᠠᠷ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠭᠰᠢᠯᠡᠭᠦᠯᠬᠦ ᠪᠠ ᠣᠷᠴᠢᠨ ᠠᠬᠤᠶ ᠶᠢ ᠬᠠᠮᠠᠭᠠᠯᠠᠬᠤ ᠠᠵᠢᠯᠯᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠠᠪᠬᠤ ᠶᠢ ᠵᠣᠷᠢᠭᠵᠢᠭᠤᠯᠬᠤ ᠭᠣᠣᠯ ᠬᠦᠴᠦᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠭᠠᠬᠤ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠬᠠᠮᠲᠤ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠬᠦ ᠴᠢᠬᠤᠯᠠ ᠨᠡᠶᠢᠭᠡᠮ ᠦᠨ ᠬᠥᠳᠡᠯᠭᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠢ ᠠᠰᠢᠭᠯᠠᠵᠤ᠂ ᠬᠥᠮᠦᠰ ᠦᠨ ᠳᠠᠯᠠᠢ ᠲᠠᠩᠭᠢᠰ ᠤᠨ ᠪᠣᠬᠢᠷᠲᠤᠯ᠂ ᠪᠦᠬᠦ ᠪᠥᠮᠪᠥᠷᠴᠡᠭ ᠦᠨ ᠳᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠᠷᠠᠯ ᠵᠡᠷᠭᠡ ᠰᠢᠨ᠎ᠡ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠪᠤᠢ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠣᠷᠴᠢᠨ ᠠᠬᠤᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠠᠰᠠᠭᠤᠳᠠᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠲᠤᠬᠠᠶ ᠲᠠᠨᠢᠯᠲᠠ ᠶᠢ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠭᠰᠢᠯᠡᠭᠦᠯᠵᠡᠶ᠃ᠣᠳᠣᠬᠠᠨ ᠳᠤ᠂ ᠪᠦᠬᠦ ᠳᠡᠯᠡᠬᠡᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤ ᠭᠠᠷᠤᠢ ᠤᠯᠤᠰ ᠵᠢᠯ ᠪᠦᠷᠢ ᠳᠡᠯᠡᠬᠡᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠣᠷᠴᠢᠨ ᠠᠬᠤᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠡᠳᠦᠷ ᠲᠦ ᠣᠷᠣᠯᠴᠠᠵᠤ᠂ ᠤᠯᠠᠨ ᠨᠡᠶᠢᠲᠡ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠨᠢᠯᠲᠠ ᠤᠬᠠᠭᠳᠠᠬᠤᠨ ᠢ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠭ᠍ᠰᠢᠯᠡᠭᠦᠯᠬᠦ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠵᠣᠷᠢᠵᠠᠢ᠃ ᠵᠢᠯ ᠪᠦᠷᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠳᠡᠯᠡᠬᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠣᠷᠴᠢᠨ ᠠᠬᠤᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠡᠳᠦᠷ ᠲᠦ ᠪᠥᠬᠥ ᠳᠡᠯᠡᠬᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠡᠯ᠎ᠡ ᠲᠣᠮᠣ ᠺᠣᠮᠫᠠᠨᠢ᠂ ᠵᠠᠰᠠᠭ ᠤᠨ ᠣᠷᠳᠣᠨ ᠤ ᠪᠤᠰᠤ ᠵᠣᠬᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠭᠤᠯᠤᠯᠲᠠ᠂ ᠡᠯ᠎ᠡ ᠲᠥᠷᠥᠯ ᠦᠨ ᠪᠦᠯᠬᠦᠮ᠂ ᠵᠠᠰᠠᠭ ᠤᠨ ᠣᠷᠳᠣᠨ ᠪᠠ ᠨᠡᠶᠢᠭᠡᠮ ᠦᠨ ᠨᠠᠷᠠᠲᠤ ᠬᠥᠮᠦᠰ ᠴᠥᠮ ᠲᠣᠰ ᠵᠢᠯ ᠦᠨ ᠰᠣᠩᠭᠣᠨ ᠲᠣᠭᠲᠠᠭᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠰᠢᠨ᠎ᠡ ᠭᠣᠸᠯ ᠰᠡᠳᠦᠪ ᠢ ᠦᠨᠳᠦᠰᠦᠯᠡᠵᠦ ᠂ ᠣᠷᠴᠢᠨ ᠠᠬᠤᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠲᠤᠬᠠᠶ ᠵᠥᠪᠯᠡᠬᠦ ᠰᠡᠳᠦᠪ ᠢ ᠢᠳᠡᠪᠬᠢᠲᠡᠶ ᠰᠠᠨᠠᠭᠠᠴᠢᠯᠠᠳᠠᠭ᠃ ᠵᠢᠱᠢᠶᠡᠯᠡᠪᠡᠯ《ᠰᠦᠯᠢᠶᠣᠣ ᠶᠢ ᠲᠡᠪᠴᠢᠬᠦ》 ᠭᠣᠣᠯ ᠰᠡᠳᠦᠪᠲᠦ ᠳᠡᠯᠡᠬᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠣᠷᠴᠢᠨ ᠠᠬᠤᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠡᠳᠦᠷ ᠰᠦᠯᠢᠶᠣᠣ  ᠶᠢ ᠪᠠᠭᠠᠰᠬᠠᠬᠤ ᠠᠵᠢᠯᠯᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ  ᠶᠢ ᠬᠥᠮᠦᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠪᠦᠷᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠡᠳᠦᠷ ᠲᠤᠲᠤᠮ ᠤᠨ ᠠᠮᠢᠳᠤᠷᠠᠯ ᠳᠤ ᠨᠠᠶᠢᠳᠠᠪᠤᠷᠢᠵᠢᠭᠤᠯᠵᠤ᠂ ᠲᠦᠷ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠷ᠎ᠠ  ᠶᠢᠨ ᠳᠥᠭᠥᠮ ᠢ ᠬᠥᠭᠡᠭᠡᠴᠡᠯᠳᠦᠬᠦ ᠳᠠᠳᠬᠠᠯ  ᠢ ᠲᠠᠶᠠᠭᠳᠠᠵᠤ᠂ ᠰᠦᠯᠢᠶᠣᠣ ᠪᠦᠲᠦᠭᠡᠭᠳᠡᠬᠦᠨ ᠬᠡᠷᠡᠭᠯᠡᠬᠦ  ᠶᠢ ᠠᠯᠢ ᠴᠢᠳᠠᠬᠤ ᠪᠠᠷ ᠪᠠᠭᠠᠰᠬᠠᠵᠤ ᠲᠤᠬᠠᠢ ᠴᠤᠤᠷᠢᠶᠠᠯᠠᠭ ᠤᠷᠢᠶᠠᠯᠠᠪᠠ᠃
mo 6 Monocole ᠳᠠᠩ ᠢᠯᠲᠠᠰᠤᠲᠤ ᠨᠢᠳᠦᠨ ᠰᠢᠯ ᠪᠣᠯ ᠵᠥᠪᠬᠡᠨ ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠨᠢᠳᠦᠨ ᠦ ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠶᠢ ᠵᠠᠯᠠᠷᠠᠭᠤᠯᠬᠤ ᠪᠤᠶᠤ ᠴᠢᠩᠭᠠᠷᠠᠭᠤᠯᠬᠤ ᠳᠤ ᠬᠡᠷᠡᠭᠯᠡᠳᠡᠭ ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠵᠦᠢᠯ ᠦᠨ ᠵᠠᠯᠠᠷᠠᠭᠤᠯᠬᠤ ᠰᠢᠯ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠨ᠎ᠠ᠃ ᠲᠡᠷᠡ ᠨᠢ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠲᠣᠭᠣᠷᠢᠭ ᠮᠡᠰᠢᠯ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠪᠦᠷᠢᠯᠳᠦᠵᠦ᠂ ᠶᠡᠷᠦ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠲᠣᠭᠣᠷᠢᠭ ᠤᠨ ᠬᠦᠷᠢᠶᠡᠨ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ᠎ᠡ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠲᠡᠮᠦᠷᠯᠢᠭ ᠭᠠᠷᠠᠬ᠎ᠠ ᠲᠠᠶ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠵᠤ᠂ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠰᠦ ᠪᠤᠶᠤ ᠲᠡᠮᠦᠷᠯᠢᠭ ᠤᠲᠠᠰᠤᠨ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ᠎ᠡ ᠵᠠᠯᠭᠠᠳᠠᠭ᠃ ᠳᠠᠷᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠨᠢ ᠭᠡᠭᠡᠬᠦ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠪᠤᠯᠭᠤᠮᠵᠢᠯᠠᠵᠤ᠂ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠰᠦᠨ ᠦ ᠨᠥᠭᠥᠭᠡ ᠦᠵᠦᠭᠦᠷ  ᠢ ᠰᠢᠯ ᠵᠡᠭᠦᠵᠤ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠬᠥᠮᠦᠨ ᠦ ᠬᠤᠪᠴᠠᠰᠤᠨ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ᠎ᠡ ᠬᠣᠯᠪᠣᠨ᠎ᠠ ᠃ ᠠᠷᠪᠠ ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠳᠦᠭᠡᠷ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠰᠡᠭᠦᠯᠴᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠦᠶ᠎ᠡ ᠳᠦ᠂ ᠳᠠᠩ ᠢᠯᠲᠠᠰᠤᠲᠤ ᠨᠢᠳᠦᠨ ᠰᠢᠯ ᠢ ᠶᠡᠷᠦ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠪᠠᠶᠠᠨ ᠴᠢᠨᠡᠭᠡᠯᠢᠭ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠳᠦ ᠳᠠᠪᠬᠤᠷᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠡᠷᠡᠭᠲᠡᠶᠢᠴᠦᠳ  ᠡᠳ᠋ᠯᠡᠳᠡᠭ ᠪᠠᠢᠵᠠᠢ᠃ ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠤᠷᠲᠤ ᠭᠠᠳᠠᠷ ᠬᠤᠪᠴᠠᠰᠤ ᠪᠠ ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠶᠣᠰᠣᠯᠠᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠮᠠᠯᠠᠭᠠᠶ ᠲᠠᠶ ᠤᠶᠠᠯᠳᠤᠭᠤᠯᠤᠨ᠂ ᠳᠠᠩ ᠨᠢᠳᠦᠨ ᠰᠢᠯ ᠨᠢ ᠠᠷᠪᠠ ᠶᠢᠰᠤᠳᠦᠭᠡᠷ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠰᠡᠭᠦᠯᠴᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠦᠶ᠎ᠡ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠬᠡᠪᠰᠢᠮᠡᠯ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠭᠳᠠᠯ ᠳᠠᠬᠢ ᠬᠥᠷᠥᠩᠭᠡᠲᠡᠨ ᠦ ᠬᠤᠪᠴᠠᠰᠤ ᠵᠠᠰᠠᠯ ᠢ ᠪᠦᠷᠢᠯᠳᠦᠭᠦᠯᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠳᠠᠩ ᠢᠯᠲᠠᠰᠤᠲᠤ ᠨᠢᠳᠦᠨ ᠰᠢᠯ ᠨᠢ ᠮᠥᠨ ᠴᠦ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠦᠶ ᠡ ᠢᠢᠨ ᠴᠡᠷᠢᠭ ᠦᠨ ᠳᠠᠷᠤᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠵᠠᠰᠠᠯ ᠴᠢᠮᠡᠭᠯᠡᠯ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠨ᠎ᠠ᠃ ᠬᠡᠳᠦᠶᠢᠪᠡᠷ ᠳᠠᠩ ᠢᠯᠲᠠᠰᠤᠲᠤ ᠨᠢᠳᠦᠨ ᠰᠢᠯ ᠠᠷᠪᠠ ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠳᠦᠭᠡᠷ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠰᠡᠭᠦᠯᠴᠢ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠶᠡᠬᠡ ᠳᠡᠯᠭᠡᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠴᠤ᠂ ᠥᠨᠥᠳᠦᠷ ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠴᠥᠭᠡᠨ ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠭᠳᠠᠬᠤ ᠪᠤᠯᠵᠠᠢ᠃ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠨᠢ ᠨᠡᠯᠢᠶᠡᠳ ᠶᠡᠬᠡ ᠬᠡᠮᠵᠢᠶᠡᠨ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ᠎ᠡ ᠪᠡᠨ ᠭᠡᠷᠡᠯ ᠰᠢᠯᠭᠠᠬᠤ ᠤᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠳᠠᠪᠰᠢᠯᠲᠠ ᠠᠴᠠ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠶᠤᠮ᠃ ᠭᠡᠷᠡᠯ ᠰᠢᠯᠭᠠᠬᠤ ᠨᠢ ᠭᠡᠷᠡᠯ ᠦᠨ ᠨᠤᠭᠤᠷᠠᠯᠲᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠵᠥᠷᠢᠶ᠎ᠡ ᠶᠢ ᠨᠡᠩ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠬᠡᠮᠵᠢᠳᠡᠭ᠃ ᠡᠶᠢᠮᠦ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠨᠢᠳᠦ ᠪᠦᠷᠢ ᠳᠦ ᠠᠳᠠᠯᠢ ᠪᠤᠰᠤ ᠬᠦᠴᠦᠯᠡᠴᠡ ᠲᠡᠶ ᠨᠢᠳᠦᠨ ᠰᠢᠯ ᠪᠠ ᠨᠢᠭᠤᠭᠳᠠᠮᠠᠯ ᠨᠢᠳᠦᠨ ᠰᠢᠯ ᠢ ᠳᠤᠬᠢᠷᠠᠭᠤᠯᠵᠤ ᠥᠭᠲᠡᠭ᠃

mo 8 Orange Juice ᠵᠦᠷᠵᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠰᠢᠭᠦᠰᠦ ᠪᠣᠯ ᠵᠦᠷᠵᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠢᠬᠠᠨ ᠳᠣᠲᠣᠷ᠎ᠠ ᠠᠴᠠ ᠰᠢᠬᠠᠵᠤ ᠭᠠᠷᠭᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠵᠢᠮᠢᠰ ᠦᠨ ᠰᠢᠭᠦᠰᠦ ᠮᠥᠨ᠃ ᠬᠤᠳᠠᠯᠳᠤᠭᠠᠴᠢᠳ ᠵᠦᠷᠵᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠰᠢᠭᠦᠰᠦ ᠶᠢ ᠬᠠᠳᠠᠭᠠᠯᠠᠬᠤ ᠬᠤᠭᠤᠴᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠶᠢ ᠤᠷᠲᠤᠳᠬᠠᠬᠤ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠲᠥᠯᠥᠭᠡ ᠵᠢᠮᠢᠰ ᠦᠨ ᠰᠢᠭᠦᠰᠦᠨ ᠳᠡᠬᠢ ᠬᠦᠴᠢᠯᠲᠥ᠋ᠷᠥᠭᠴᠢ ᠶᠢ ᠨᠢ ᠠᠷᠢᠯᠭᠠᠵᠤ ᠪᠠᠺᠲ᠋ᠧᠷᠢ ᠶᠢ ᠨᠢ ᠠᠯᠠᠳᠠᠭ᠂ ᠭᠡᠪᠡᠴᠦ ᠡᠨᠡ ᠨᠢ ᠵᠢᠮᠢᠰ ᠦᠨ ᠰᠢᠭᠦᠰᠦ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠠᠮᠲᠠ ᠶᠢ ᠶᠡᠬᠡ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠪᠠᠭᠤᠷᠠᠭᠤᠯᠬᠤ ᠲᠤᠯᠠ ᠶᠡᠷᠦ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠨ ᠦᠨᠦᠷᠲᠦ ᠡᠳ᠋ ᠨᠡᠮᠡᠵᠦ ᠤᠷᠤᠭᠤᠯᠳᠠᠭ᠃ ᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠭᠠᠳᠠᠨ᠎ᠠ᠂ ᠵᠠᠷᠢᠮ ᠵᠢᠮᠢᠰ ᠦᠨ ᠰᠢᠭᠦᠰᠦ ᠶᠢ ᠬᠠᠳᠠᠭᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠳᠠᠷᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠤᠰᠤᠵᠢᠭᠤᠯᠵᠤ᠂ ᠡᠰᠡᠭᠦᠯ ᠡ ᠠᠭᠰᠢᠭᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠳᠠᠷᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠤᠰᠤ ᠨᠡᠮᠡᠵᠦ ᠤᠯᠠᠮ ᠨᠢᠭᠡ ᠠᠯᠬᠤᠮ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠰᠤᠷᠠᠭᠤᠯᠳᠠᠭ᠃ ᠬᠡᠳᠦᠶᠢᠪᠡᠷ ᠵᠦᠷᠵᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠰᠢᠭᠦᠰᠦᠨ ᠳᠦ ᠶᠡᠬᠡ ᠬᠡᠮᠵᠢᠶᠡᠨ ᠦ ᠸᠢᠲ᠋ᠠᠮᠢᠨ ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠵᠤ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠬᠤ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠴᠤ ᠪᠠᠰᠠ ᠪᠣᠯᠪᠠᠴᠤ ᠪᠠᠰᠠ ᠮᠠᠰᠢ ᠥᠨᠳᠥᠷ ᠥᠳᠬᠡᠴᠡ ᠲᠡᠶ ᠲᠠᠩ ᠰᠢᠬᠢᠷ ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠵᠤ᠂ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠯᠡᠨ ᠤᠮᠳᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠳᠤᠲᠠᠭᠤ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ ᠪᠠᠢᠳᠠᠭ᠃ ᠡᠶᠢᠮᠦ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠂ ᠵᠠᠷᠢᠮ ᠵᠠᠰᠠᠭ ᠤᠨ ᠣᠷᠳᠣᠨ ᠰᠢᠮ᠎ᠡ ᠲᠡᠵᠢᠭᠡᠯ ᠦᠨ ᠰᠠᠨᠠᠭᠤᠯᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠳᠤ ᠪᠡᠨ ᠲᠣᠬᠢᠷᠠᠭᠤᠯᠤᠯᠲᠠ ᠬᠢᠵᠦ ᠂ ᠰᠢᠩᠭᠡᠭᠡᠯᠲᠡ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠤᠳᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠰᠢᠭ᠋ ᠲᠦᠭᠦᠬᠡᠶ ᠵᠢᠮᠢᠰ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠵᠦᠷᠵᠢ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠰᠢᠭᠦᠰᠦ ᠶᠢ ᠣᠷᠣᠯᠠᠭᠤᠯᠬᠤ ᠶᠢ ᠵᠣᠷᠢᠭᠵᠢᠭᠤᠯᠬᠤ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠬᠠᠮᠲᠤ ᠡᠳᠦᠷ ᠪᠤᠯᠭᠠᠨ ᠢᠳᠡᠬᠦ ᠶᠢ ᠬᠢᠵᠠᠭᠠᠷᠯᠠᠵᠠᠶ ᠃
mo 9 Beekeeping ᠪᠠᠯᠲᠤ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ  ᠶᠢ ᠲᠡᠵᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠦᠷᠡᠵᠢᠭᠦᠯᠬᠦ ᠭᠡᠳᠡᠭ ᠨᠢ ᠬᠥᠮᠦᠨ ᠦ ᠬᠦᠴᠦ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠪᠠᠯᠲᠤ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠶᠢ ᠲᠡᠵᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠦᠷᠡᠵᠢᠭᠦᠯᠬᠦ  ᠶᠢ ᠬᠡᠯᠡᠨ᠎ᠡ᠃ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠨ ᠦ ᠠᠵᠤ ᠠᠬᠤᠶ  ᠶᠢᠨ ᠦᠨ᠎ᠡ ᠥᠷᠲᠡᠭ ᠲᠦ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠪᠠᠯ᠂ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠡᠭᠦᠷ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠠᠪᠴᠤ ᠭᠠᠷᠭᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠯᠡ ᠵᠡᠷᠭᠡ ᠪᠦᠲᠦᠭᠡᠭᠳᠡᠬᠦᠨ ᠪᠠᠭᠲᠠᠨ᠎ᠠ᠃ ᠲᠡᠵᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠦᠷᠡᠵᠢᠭᠦᠯᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠪᠠᠯᠲᠤ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠨᠢ ᠪᠠᠰᠠ ᠲᠠᠷᠢᠮᠠᠯ ᠳᠤ ᠲᠣᠭᠣᠰᠣ ᠬᠦᠷᠲᠡᠭᠡᠵᠦ᠂ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ  ᠶᠢᠨ ᠴᠢᠬᠢ ᠶᠢ ᠪᠤᠰᠤᠳ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠲᠡᠵᠢᠭᠡᠭᠴᠢ ᠳᠦ ᠬᠤᠳᠠᠯᠳᠤᠨ ᠥᠭᠴᠦ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠨ᠎ᠠ᠃ ᠡᠷᠲᠡᠨ ᠦ ᠶᠧᠵᠢᠫᠲ ᠲᠦ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨᠲᠡ ᠪᠠᠯᠲᠤ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠶᠢ ᠲᠡᠵᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠦᠷᠡᠵᠢᠭᠦᠯᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠲᠡᠦᠬᠡ ᠲᠡᠶ ᠪᠣᠯᠵᠠᠶ᠃ ᠳᠥᠷᠪᠡᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠭᠠᠷᠤᠶ ᠵᠢᠯ ᠦᠨ ᠡᠮᠦᠨᠡᠬᠢ ᠶᠧᠵᠢᠫᠲ ᠦᠨ ᠤᠷᠠᠯᠢᠭ ᠠᠴᠠ ᠬᠥᠮᠦᠰ ᠳᠥᠭᠥᠮᠬᠡᠨ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠡᠭᠦᠷ ᠪᠠ ᠤᠲᠤᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠤᠨᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠢᠶᠠᠷ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠶᠢ ᠲᠡᠵᠢᠭᠡᠵᠦ ᠂ ᠪᠠᠯ ᠢ ᠯᠣᠩᠬᠣᠨ ᠳᠤ ᠬᠠᠳᠠᠭᠠᠯᠠᠵᠤ ᠂ ᠵᠠᠷᠢᠮ ᠨᠢᠭᠲᠠ ᠪᠢᠲᠡᠭᠦᠮᠵᠢᠯᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠪᠠᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠰᠠᠪᠠ  ᠶᠢ ᠪᠠᠰᠠ ᠬᠣᠶᠢᠯᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠡᠳ᠋ ᠪᠣᠯᠭᠠᠨ ᠪᠤᠯᠠᠰᠢᠨ ᠳᠤ ᠲᠠᠯᠪᠢᠵᠤ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠢ ᠣᠯᠵᠤ ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠵᠤ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠨ᠎ᠠ᠃ ᠡᠷᠲᠡᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠤᠯᠠᠮᠵᠢᠯᠠᠭᠳᠠᠨ ᠢᠷᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠬᠥᠮᠦᠨ ᠦ ᠬᠦᠴᠦ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠶᠢ ᠲᠡᠵᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠦᠷᠡᠵᠢᠭᠦᠯᠬᠦ ᠠᠷᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠮᠠᠶ᠋ᠢᠭ ᠨᠢ ᠠᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠨᠠᠢᠮᠠᠳᠤᠭᠠᠷ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠤ ᠦᠶ᠎ᠡ ᠬᠦᠷᠲᠡᠯ᠎ᠡ ᠬᠡᠷᠡᠭᠯᠡᠭᠳᠡᠵᠦ᠂ ᠬᠥᠮᠦᠰ ᠦᠨ ᠪᠠᠯᠲᠤ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠪᠸᠯᠤᠬᠢ  ᠢᠢᠨ ᠲᠤᠬᠠᠶ ᠣᠶᠢᠯᠠᠭᠠᠯᠲᠠ ᠨᠢ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠭᠰᠢᠯᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠧᠦ᠋ᠷᠣᠫᠠ ᠲᠢᠪ ᠲᠦ ᠰᠢᠯᠵᠢᠭᠦᠯᠵᠤ ᠪᠣᠯᠬᠤ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠬᠠᠢᠷᠴᠠᠭ ᠡᠭᠦᠳᠴᠦ᠂ ᠬᠦᠮᠦᠰ ᠪᠦᠬᠦᠶᠢᠯᠡ ᠵᠥᠭᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠰᠦᠷᠦᠭ ᠢ ᠡᠪᠳᠡᠬᠦ ᠦᠭᠡᠶ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠳᠠᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠳᠣᠣᠷ᠎ᠠ ᠵᠦᠭᠡᠢ ᠢᠢᠨ ᠪᠠᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠬᠤᠷᠢᠶᠠᠯᠲᠠ ᠤᠯᠬᠤ ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠨ᠎ᠠ᠃ ᠣᠷᠴᠢᠮ ᠤᠨ ᠰᠤᠳᠤᠯᠭᠠᠨ ᠳᠤ ᠢᠯᠡᠷᠡᠭᠦᠯᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ᠂ ᠵᠥᠬᠡᠶ ᠲᠡᠵᠢᠭᠡᠭᠴᠢ ᠵᠥᠬᠡᠶ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠬᠣᠸᠷ  ᠢ ᠡᠰᠡᠷᠭᠦᠴᠡᠬᠦ ᠪᠣᠳᠠᠰ ᠤᠨ ᠪᠡᠶ᠎ᠡ ᠳᠤ ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠬᠤ ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠤᠭᠳᠠᠴᠠ ᠨᠢ ᠡᠩ ᠦᠨ ᠬᠥᠮᠦᠨ ᠦ ᠬᠢ ᠡᠴᠡ ᠥᠨᠳᠥᠷ ᠪᠠᠶᠢᠳᠠᠭ᠃

01_change log.xlsx

release version version availability date (yyyy_mm_dd) version notes
1 1 2022_01_11 public release of first MECO L1 data repository. See publication: https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13428-021-01772-6
NA 1.1000000000000001 2022_02_25 Minor corrections of interest areas in the English portion of joint_data_trimmed. Additional file with comprehension questions. All other files are identical to version 1.0.0
NA 1.2 2022_07_17 Minor corrections of interest areas numbering and their assignment to sentence numbers in Estonian and English (via popEye); Correction of passage numbers in sentence- and passage-level dataframes in Estonian and Italian; Correction of Big5 scoring in Estonian individual differences. Note an issue in two interest areas in Turkish: ‘simge”ye’ and ‘Listesi”ni’. These were presented incorrectly to participants due to parsing error.
NA NA 2023_03_22 Addition to version 1.2: Fixation report (see primary data/fixation report)
NA 1.3 2025_03_20 Unification of the line assignment, sentence segmentation and hyphenation settings. Addition of saccade measures and saccade report. Correction to sentence numbering in fixation reports. Updates to popeye processing pipelines
2 2 2025_06_05 New L2 data from wave 2 of the MECO project (sub-folder “wave 2”) - paper to appear soon in Scientific Data! Wave 1 data is included in “wave 1” sub-folder; wave 1 data is identical to version 1.3
NA related_resources 2023_03_23 Addition of the folder related_resources. Addition of word length and frequency data for all L1 texts.
NA 2.1 2026_02_19 corrections of sentence reports; minor changes to comprehension datasets; minor updates to popeye processing pipelines; changes to processing fixation and saccade reports for simplified and traditional Chinese data

Descriptives Overview

We found 358 columns with at least one missing value. 129 columns are empty (no values in any row); store data without empty columns.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 1310 columns across 91 data files.

Issues Identified

226 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 91 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 4 R scripts and 1 Python script in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. 4 identical copies of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, were not run again.

1 of 5 scripts ran to the end: 4 did not reproduce.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • release 1.0/version 1.0/code/supp-code-r1.R reads cft.all.2021may20.csv.
  • analyses_and_plots.ipynb reads Bao_et_al_2025.csv.
  • supp-code.R reads cft.all.2020may8.csv.
  • Main.R reads descriptive_eyemove_language.csv.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 2 statistical tests reported in the paper, 0 were found in the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 4 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 release 1.0/version 1.0/code/supp-code-r1.R — numeric
2 release 1.0/version 1.2/code/supp-code-r1.R — numeric
3 supp-code.R — none
4 Main.R supp-code.R dependency

File paths

The data paths in the code to files the repository holds work as deposited, but 3 paths name a file the repository does not hold: by_sub_meco.rda, cft.all.2021may20.csv, cft.all.2020may8.csv. 1 reference matched several files sharing a name and could not be resolved by study group or folder; it was left unrewritten and flagged.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 3 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: by_sub_meco.rda, cft.all.2021may20.csv, cft.all.2020may8.csv.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 1 ran without error, 3 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

Duplicate files across repo mirrors

4 files are byte-identical to another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component that mirrors the same materials). They were only run once, from its first occurrence, to avoid wasted duplicate execution: supp-code-r1.R at https://osf.io/download/hej9s/ (same as supp-code-r1.R at https://osf.io/download/7h3cu/); supp-code-r1.R at https://osf.io/download/ky6dw/ (same as supp-code-r1.R at https://osf.io/download/7nbd4/); supp-code.R at https://osf.io/download/ghj2s/ (same as supp-code.R at https://osf.io/download/rkp6c/); supp-code.R at https://osf.io/download/p5k8y/ (same as supp-code.R at https://osf.io/download/rkp6c/).

Python code

This module also assesses whether the paper’s Python code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 1 Python code file.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no source()-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an import loads a module, not the paper’s own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 0 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt).
